global.headline: UAE SAYS IRAN FIRED BALLISTIC MISSILES AT ITS TERRITORY AS TRUMP ORDERS ENVOYS TO HALT TALKS, DOJ UNSEALS EXPANDED IRANIAN HACKING INDICTMENT
summary: The UAE said Tuesday its air defences detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran toward the country — the first such barrage aimed at the UAE in months — with one falling outside its territorial waters and the second within them; both were aimed at "maritime navigation" and caused no damage. The alert came nearly two hours after a brief phone warning to residents of a "potential missile threat." Iran's foreign ministry dismissed the accusation as "baseless." The claim and counter-claim land a day after the 17 June MOU's 60-day ceasefire-extension window lapsed without resolution.

Separately, Trump has told his top envoys to halt conversations with Iran altogether, according to a US official — a marked shift from months of insisting a deal was imminent to declaring no diplomacy is underway at all. Allies briefed by the White House describe the pivot as moving from "hammer Iran ASAP" to "strangle them" over time: a longer-term economic-containment approach rather than active negotiation or a fresh strike campaign. Omani officials and observers, meanwhile, remained visibly angered and puzzled by Monday's threat to "bomb the [expletive] out of" Oman if it "gets in the way" of a Hormuz deal — a threat aimed at the one mediator still holding a working channel to Tehran.

The Justice Department separately unsealed an expanded indictment charging eight more Iranian nationals — bringing the total to 17, including nine charged back in 2018 — over a years-long hacking campaign run on behalf of the IRGC-linked Mabna Institute. Prosecutors say the group stole roughly 31.5 terabytes of data from 144 US and 178 foreign universities, 42 US and 11 foreign companies, and five US government agencies, and are offering a US$10 million reward for five still-at-large defendants. Brent crude extended its climb to roughly US$91–92/barrel (S$123–124), continuing gains on fading hopes of any near-term Hormuz breakthrough.
global.geopolitical: A president publicly disengaging from talks while a Gulf ally reports its first Iranian missile fire in months, and prosecutors unveil the scale of a parallel IRGC cyber campaign against Western universities and agencies, together describe a war settling into indefinite, multi-front attrition rather than moving toward any negotiated close.
global.socioeconomic: Oil's steady climb toward US$92/barrel as ceasefire hopes fade keeps compounding costs across shipping insurance, fuel and freight for economies far from the Gulf, while Trump's own account of a shift to slow economic strangulation signals Washington now expects the pressure — and the price pain — to be measured in months, not days.

global.headline: ZAMBIA'S ELECTORAL COMMISSION FORMALLY DECLARES HICHILEMA WINNER WITH 60.49% AS RIVAL MUNDUBILE GOES INTO HIDING FEARING ARREST
summary: Zambia's Electoral Commission declared President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of a second term on Tuesday, with final consolidated results from all 226 constituencies showing 2,965,326 votes (60.49%) against challenger Brian Mundubile's 1,856,217 votes (37.87%) — a clear first-round majority that avoids a run-off. Commission chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis formally pronounced Hichilema "president-elect of the Republic of Zambia this 18th day of August, 2026."

Mundubile's New Revolutionary Republican Progressive United Party said he has gone into hiding at a location protected by an international human rights body, fearing arrest, after Friday's raid on his Kabulonga residence — which the government said uncovered a militia cell with "high-grade military weapons" and which Mundubile has called fabricated. He said he will mount a legal challenge, citing evidence of voting irregularities.
global.geopolitical: A decisive, first-round margin gives Hichilema a stronger mandate than a contested run-off would have, but a losing candidate driven into hiding by alleged arrest threats, on the same day the result is certified, hands international observers a harder story to wave away than a bare vote tally ever did.
global.socioeconomic: Certainty over the presidency removes one source of investor uncertainty for an economy Hichilema has steadily steered through recovery, but a legal challenge layered on top of an opposition figure in hiding risks keeping that uncertainty alive well past the declared result.

global.headline: ZIMBABWE'S KARIBA FERRY DEATH TOLL CLIMBS TO 93 AS RECOVERY CONTINUES
summary: The death toll from the 11 August capsizing of the government-operated ferry Mbuya Nehanda on Lake Kariba rose to 93 on Tuesday, Zimbabwe Republic Police said, after another body was recovered on an island — up from 84 reported Monday. It remains the deadliest transport disaster in Zimbabwe's history. Police have released the names of 39 victims positively identified by next of kin so far.

The state-run Rural Infrastructure Development Agency vessel was licensed to carry 90 people but had an estimated 168–170 aboard, including crew, when it was struck by a strong wave on the Kariba-Chalala route; 77 people survived.
global.geopolitical: Each upward toll revision keeps pressure on Harare's transport-safety oversight of state-run ferry services in the international spotlight.
global.socioeconomic: With the death toll now more than double the initial count and still being confirmed through identification of remains, the disaster's economic shadow over the lake's remote, road-scarce communities — who depend on the ferry route for trade and travel — deepens along with the toll itself.

global.headline: STUDENT GUNMAN KILLS CLASSMATE, HIMSELF AT PHILIPPINE CATHOLIC UNIVERSITY IN SECOND SCHOOL SHOOTING IN TWO MONTHS
summary: A seventh-grade student brought a high-powered firearm and a .45-calibre pistol into Ateneo de Zamboanga University, a Catholic private school in the southern Philippines, on Tuesday. Authorities say he first fired at a teacher seated at a table but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a fellow student, who later died of injuries; the gunman then killed himself.
It is the Philippines' second school shooting in as many months, intensifying scrutiny of campus security and firearm access in the country's schools.
global.geopolitical: A second fatal school shooting inside two months sharpens regional attention on the Philippines' gun-control and school-security regime, an issue with resonance across Southeast Asia's own campus-safety debates.
global.socioeconomic: Recurring campus violence pressures Philippine schools — Catholic private institutions included — toward costlier security upgrades just as many already face tight post-pandemic budgets.

global.headline: ISRAEL STRIKES SYRIAN AIR BASE NEAR TURKISH BORDER, US ENVOY CALLS IT 'UNNECESSARY ESCALATION'
summary: Israel carried out eight airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur air base in Syria's Idlib province, roughly 70km from the Turkish border, hitting the runway and storage facilities, Syria's military said. US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said Tuesday the strikes constitute an "unnecessary escalation" that does not advance regional stability, adding Washington was "deeply concerned" and urging all parties toward "logical discourse."

Barrack said Syria's interim government under President Ahmad al-Sharaa has "neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces" and has repeatedly signalled a preference for de-escalation with Israel — a rare direct US rebuke of an Israeli strike this year.
global.geopolitical: A US envoy publicly rebuking an Israeli strike as unnecessary, on a government Washington has been courting toward normalisation, exposes daylight between the allies at a moment already strained by Gaza's stalled peace process and the Iran war's own US-Israel friction.
global.socioeconomic: Repeated Israeli strikes inside Syria complicate international reconstruction and investment interest in Syria's fragile post-Assad transition, undercutting exactly the stability Washington says it is trying to encourage.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE ORDERS SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS TO VERIFY ADVERTISERS' IDENTITIES AGAINST GOVERNMENT RECORDS UNDER NEW ANTI-SCAM CODE
summary: The Singapore Police Force issued new Codes of Practice under the Online Criminal Harms Act on Monday, including a new Code for Social Media Services that replaces the existing Code for Online Communication Services. Designated platforms — covering Facebook, Instagram and TikTok — must verify advertisers' identities against government records and screen ads for scam indicators such as URL cloaking, with compliance required by 31 January 2027; failure is a criminal offence carrying fines of up to $1 million.

The tightened rules follow data showing Facebook, Instagram and TikTok together accounted for roughly 30% of Singapore's scam cases in 2025, with Facebook alone responsible for about 18%. Home Affairs and Law Minister K Shanmugam separately told an MHA scholarship event Monday evening that internet-enabled scams and AI pose growing challenges, adding that MHA agencies are themselves now using AI to detect and fight crime.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic regulatory matter, though it adds Singapore to a small group of jurisdictions imposing binding advertiser-verification duties directly on major US social platforms.
singapore.socioeconomic: Compliance costs and criminal liability now fall squarely on platforms rather than victims, but the 31 January 2027 runway means today's scam-advertising exposure on these apps continues largely unchanged for several more months.

singapore.headline: MUIS TO REVIEW MOSQUE SAFEGUARDS AFTER 'RELIGIOUS INFLUENCER' JAILED 27 YEARS FOR ABUSING BOYS AT MOSQUE
summary: Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs Zaqy Mohamad has instructed the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) to review its safeguards after a 37-year-old self-styled "religious influencer" was sentenced Monday to 27 years and 10 months' jail plus 24 strokes of the cane for sexually abusing two brothers between 2022 and 2023 — including repeated rape of the younger boy, then aged six to eight, at several locations, among them a mosque toilet where the pair often prayed together.

MUIS said the man's informal religious classes were not sanctioned by the mosque, but will nonetheless strengthen security — including patrols and CCTV monitoring — and review safeguards around informal activities and gatherings involving children and youths, particularly as more religious engagement moves online.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic child-safety and religious-institution governance matter.
singapore.socioeconomic: A conviction this severe for abuse enabled by unsupervised access to children at a place of worship puts pressure on all of Singapore's religious institutions, not just mosques, to tighten vetting of informal, unofficial activity happening on or near their premises.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE'S FOREIGN-WORKER GAMBLING SELF-EXCLUSIONS HAVE RISEN, MOSTLY EMPLOYER-INITIATED
summary: The number of foreign workers excluding themselves from Singapore's casinos has grown in recent years, the National Council on Problem Gambling's data shows, with the uptick driven mainly by employers applying for group exclusions on workers' behalf, with the workers' consent, rather than by workers self-applying individually. Migrant-worker volunteer "ambassadors" have also emerged to help peers use self-exclusion to curb problematic gambling.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic social-policy and migrant-worker welfare matter.
singapore.socioeconomic: Employer-driven exclusion suggests companies are increasingly treating workers' gambling risk as a workplace welfare issue rather than leaving it purely to individual choice, though it also raises questions about how genuinely voluntary consent is within an employer-employee relationship.

singapore.headline: NEW MARINE PARADE YOUTH DIGITAL-WELLNESS CENTRE OPENS AS SURVEY FINDS PARENTS STRUGGLING WITH CHILDREN'S ONLINE AND MENTAL HEALTH NEEDS
summary: DigitallyUs@Marine Parade, described as Singapore's first integrated centre for youth digital wellness and mental health support, opened this week. Its accompanying survey found parents reporting difficulty keeping up with both their children's digital habits and mental health needs, underscoring the case for a dedicated, combined support service rather than treating the two issues separately.
singapore.socioeconomic: A purpose-built centre addressing digital and mental wellbeing together reflects growing recognition that youth online-harm and mental-health support in Singapore have outgrown generic counselling services, though its Marine Parade location means reach beyond that catchment remains to be seen.

word.definition: At the point of death; lacking vitality, vigour or the capacity to develop further, as if dying.
word.etymology: From Latin moribundus, "dying," from mori, "to die"; entered English in the late 18th century.
word.example: With Trump ordering his envoys to stop talking to Tehran altogether and pivoting from "hammer Iran ASAP" to a slow economic strangulation, the US-Iran diplomatic track looked entirely moribund — no talks, no deadline, just an open-ended war of attrition.
